passages.happening:
In the church at Antioch there are prophets and teachers: Barnabas, Simeon called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen, who had been brought up with Herod the tetrarch, and Saul (verse 1).

While they are worshipping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit says, “Set apart for Me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them” (verse 2). So after more fasting and prayer, they lay their hands on the two and send them off (verse 3).
passages.hearers:
Look at the list of leaders. Barnabas is a Levite from Cyprus. Simeon is ‘called Niger’, a Latin word meaning ‘black’, perhaps because of his skin; some think he came from Africa. Lucius is from Cyrene, in North Africa. Manaen grew up with Herod the tetrarch, the Herod Antipas who killed John the Baptist, so he came from the world of the royal court. Saul is a former Pharisee from Tarsus. The church at Antioch is led by a mixed group of men from different lands and different classes. Its leadership looks like its message.

They are ‘worshipping the Lord and fasting’. Fasting means going without food for a time, to give full attention to God. The call comes in worship, not in a planning meeting.

‘Set apart’ means to separate for a task, to dedicate. Barnabas and Saul are the church's best teachers, and the church gives them away.

Laying on hands was a sign of blessing and of sending. It did not make them apostles or give them a power they lacked. It showed that the whole church stood behind them. This is the start of what readers often call Paul's first missionary trip, told in chapters 13 and 14. Counting back from the one firm date in Paul's travels (Gallio, about AD 51 to 52, in 18:12), many place it in the later 40s, but the exact years are not known.
passages.ot:
The Spirit's words, ‘Set apart for Me’, use the language of holiness in the Old Testament. God set apart the Levites to serve him (Numbers 8:14), and Israel itself was set apart: “I have set you apart from the nations to be My own” (Leviticus 20:26). Now two men are set apart, not from the nations, but for them.

Laying hands on those sent goes back to Moses, who laid his hands on Joshua before the whole people (Numbers 27:18-20), and to the laying of hands on the Levites (Numbers 8:10).
passages.asks: The church at Antioch heard God's call while it was worshipping and fasting, and it gave away its two best teachers. Ask whether your church is willing to send its best, not keep them. And ask whether you are close enough to God, in worship and prayer, to hear where he is sending you.

passages.t: Cyprus: the proconsul and the sorcerer
passages.happening:
Sent by the Holy Spirit, Barnabas and Saul go down to Seleucia and sail to Cyprus (verse 4). At Salamis they preach in the Jewish synagogues, with John as their helper (verse 5).

They cross the whole island to Paphos. There they meet “a Jewish sorcerer and false prophet named Bar-Jesus” (verse 6), who is an attendant of the proconsul, Sergius Paulus. The proconsul, “a man of intelligence”, sends for Barnabas and Saul because he wants to hear the word of God (verse 7). But Elymas the sorcerer opposes them and tries to turn the proconsul from the faith (verse 8).

“Then Saul, who was also called Paul”, filled with the Holy Spirit, looks straight at him (verse 9). He calls him an enemy of all righteousness, full of deceit, and asks, “Will you never stop perverting the straight ways of the Lord?” (verse 10). The hand of the Lord is against him, Paul says, and for a time he will be blind. At once mist and darkness come over him, and he gropes about for someone to lead him by the hand (verse 11).

When the proconsul sees what has happened, he believes, “for he was astonished at the teaching about the Lord” (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
Seleucia was the port of Antioch. Cyprus was Barnabas's home island. Salamis was its main city on the east coast; Paphos, on the west coast, was where the Roman governor lived.

Notice where they start: ‘in the Jewish synagogues’. That will be Paul's pattern in town after town. The good news is about Israel's Messiah, and it goes to Israel first.

A proconsul was the governor of a province that the Roman senate oversaw, appointed usually for a year. Luke uses the right title for Cyprus at this time. An inscription found in Rome names a Lucius Sergius Paullus as one of the officials in charge of the banks of the river Tiber under the emperor Claudius. Some scholars think he was this same man, before or after his time in Cyprus. That has been suggested with good reasons, but it is not certain.

Bar-Jesus means ‘son of Jesus’ (or ‘son of Joshua’), a common Jewish name. Luke also calls him Elymas, and says this name means ‘sorcerer’; how the two names connect is not clear. Important Romans sometimes kept such advisers, who claimed to read the stars or work magic. The man who opposes the message about Jesus bears the name ‘son of Jesus’.

Then a small phrase with a big place in the book: ‘Saul, who was also called Paul’. This is not a new name given at his conversion. Saul had both names already, as many Jews outside the land did: a Hebrew name, Saul, the name of Israel's first king, who like Paul was of the tribe of Benjamin (Philippians 3:5), and a Roman name, Paul (Paulus). The Greek phrase is the ordinary way of saying ‘also known as’, as with ‘John, also called Mark’ (12:12). From here on, as the mission moves into the Greek and Roman world, Luke uses his Roman name, and Paul leads: it is now ‘Paul and Barnabas’.

Paul himself was once blinded on the road to Damascus and led by the hand (9:8). Now a man who is fighting the truth is blinded ‘for a time’. Paul knew what that darkness was like, and that it could end in sight.
passages.ot:
The Law of Moses forbade sorcery and the reading of omens (Deuteronomy 18:10-11), and it warned against a false prophet who leads people away from the LORD (Deuteronomy 13:5).

Paul's words, ‘perverting the straight ways of the Lord’, echo the prophets. Isaiah called for a straight way for the LORD in the wilderness (Isaiah 40:3), and Hosea says, “the ways of the LORD are right” (Hosea 14:9). Elymas makes crooked what God has made straight.

Blindness as a judgment that brings people to a stop appears in the Law (Deuteronomy 28:28) and in the story of Elisha, when God struck an enemy army with blindness and Elisha led them where he wished (2 Kings 6:18-20). In both, the blindness was not the end: the army was fed and sent home.
passages.asks: Sergius Paulus wanted to hear the word of God, and someone close to him tried to stop him. Ask who, or what, stands between the people you know and a fair hearing of the good news. And notice the proconsul: an intelligent, powerful man, ‘astonished at the teaching’. Faith and a good mind are not enemies.

passages.happening:
From Paphos, Paul and his companions sail to Perga in Pamphylia, “where John left them to return to Jerusalem” (verse 13). From Perga they travel inland to Pisidian Antioch. On the Sabbath they go into the synagogue and sit down (verse 14).

After the reading from the Law and the Prophets, the synagogue leaders send word: “Brothers, if you have a word of encouragement for the people, please speak” (verse 15).

Paul stands up, motions with his hand, and begins: “Men of Israel and you Gentiles who fear God, listen to me!” (verse 16). He tells Israel's story. God chose their fathers, made them a great people in Egypt, and led them out “with an uplifted arm” (verse 17). He bore with them forty years in the wilderness and gave them the land. He gave them judges, then King Saul, and then David, of whom God said, ‘I have found David son of Jesse a man after My own heart’ (verse 22). “From the descendants of this man, God has brought to Israel the Savior Jesus, as He promised” (verse 23). John prepared the way, saying that one was coming after him “whose sandals I am not worthy to untie” (verse 25).
passages.hearers:
Perga was a city near the south coast of what is now Turkey. Pisidian Antioch was far inland, over the Taurus Mountains. It was a Roman colony: the emperor Augustus had settled army veterans from Italy there, and it belonged to the Roman province of Galatia. (It is a different city from Antioch in Syria, where the church sent them out.)

John Mark goes home. Luke does not say why. Later, Paul refuses to take him on another trip because ‘he had deserted them in Pamphylia’, and Paul and Barnabas part over it (15:37-39). Years later, Paul writes, ‘Get Mark and bring him with you, because he is useful to me in the ministry’ (2 Timothy 4:11). A young man who turned back was not finished.

The synagogue service Luke describes fits what is known of synagogues of the time: Scripture read from the Law (the five books of Moses) and the Prophets, and then a ‘word of encouragement’, a sermon, often from a visiting teacher. Jesus did the same at Nazareth (Luke 4:16-17). The ‘synagogue leaders’ arranged the service.

Paul speaks to two groups: ‘Men of Israel’, and ‘Gentiles who fear God’. The second group are people like Cornelius (10:2), Gentiles who worshipped Israel's God and came to the synagogue without becoming Jews.

He starts where his hearers start: their own story, from Egypt to David. He is a Jew speaking to Jews about their shared history, and he presents Jesus as its promised end.
passages.ot:
Paul's retelling runs through the Old Testament. God led Israel out of Egypt with a strong arm: “I will redeem you with an outstretched arm and with mighty acts of judgment” (Exodus 6:6). The forty years in the wilderness, the land, the judges and Samuel, King Saul of the tribe of Benjamin, and then David.

Paul's words about David join two passages. Samuel told Saul, “the LORD has sought a man after His own heart” (1 Samuel 13:14), and a psalm says, “I have found My servant David; with My sacred oil I have anointed him” (Psalm 89:20).

Then the promise: a son of David would rule forever (2 Samuel 7:12-16). Paul's whole point is that the promise has come true in Jesus.
passages.asks: Paul began with the story his hearers knew and loved, and showed them where it led. Ask whether you know the Old Testament story well enough to see Jesus as its goal. And remember John Mark. If you have turned back from something God gave you to do, your story is not over.

passages.happening:
“Brothers, children of Abraham, and you Gentiles who fear God,” Paul says, “it is to us that this message of salvation has been sent” (verse 26).

The people of Jerusalem and their rulers did not recognize Jesus, yet in condemning him they fulfilled the words of the prophets read every Sabbath (verse 27). Though they found no ground for a death sentence, they asked Pilate to have him executed. They took him down from the tree and laid him in a tomb (verses 28-29). “But God raised Him from the dead” (verse 30), and for many days he was seen by those who had come with him from Galilee.

Paul quotes the Psalms and the Prophets: ‘You are My Son; today I have become Your Father’; ‘I will give you the holy and sure blessings promised to David’; ‘You will not let Your Holy One see decay’ (verses 33-35). David died and saw decay. “But the One whom God raised from the dead did not see decay” (verse 37).

“Therefore let it be known to you, brothers, that through Jesus the forgiveness of sins is proclaimed to you” (verse 38). “Through Him everyone who believes is justified from everything you could not be justified from by the law of Moses” (verse 39). Paul ends with a warning from the prophets: “For I am doing a work in your days that you would never believe, even if someone told you” (verse 41).
passages.hearers:
Paul calls his hearers ‘brothers, children of Abraham’. He is one of them. When he says ‘the people of Jerusalem and their rulers’ did not recognize Jesus, he is speaking about one city's leaders and crowd, years before, to Jews far away in another land, and in the same breath he offers them forgiveness. He even says they acted in a way that fulfilled the prophets. The note on Acts 2:22-28 explains why such words must never be turned against the Jewish people.

The argument from the Psalm is simple. David wrote, ‘You will not let Your Holy One see decay.’ But David died, was buried, and his body decayed. So the promise must be about someone else: the son of David whom God raised, whose body did not decay.

Then comes the word ‘justified’, for the first time in Acts. It comes from the law court, where a judge ‘justifies’ someone by declaring him in the right. Paul says that through Jesus everyone who believes is ‘justified’, set right with God, in a way the law of Moses could not do.

Paul does not say the Law was bad. He says it could not do this one thing: clear a guilty person completely before God. Only forgiveness through Jesus can.
passages.ot:
Paul builds his case on three Old Testament passages. First, the second Psalm: “You are My Son; today I have become Your Father” (Psalm 2:7). Paul reads the resurrection as the day God publicly named Jesus his Son and King.

Second, Isaiah's promise of an everlasting covenant: “I will make with you an everlasting covenant” (Isaiah 55:3), the faithful love promised to David.

Third, Psalm 16: “You will not abandon my soul to Sheol, nor will You let Your Holy One see decay” (Psalm 16:10). Peter used the same psalm at Pentecost (2:25-31).

The warning at the end is from Habakkuk, who warned his people that God was doing something they would not believe: “For I am doing a work in your days that you would never believe even if someone told you” (Habakkuk 1:5).

And ‘justified’ has Old Testament roots: “Abram believed the LORD, and it was credited to him as righteousness” (Genesis 15:6).
passages.hard: How do Christians read the word ‘justified’ (verse 39)? They have understood it in different ways, and the differences are real. Lutheran and Reformed churches teach that God declares the sinner righteous for Christ's sake, a verdict received by faith alone, and that a new life follows from it. The Catholic Church teaches, in words its Catechism takes from the Council of Trent, that justification ‘is not only the remission of sins, but also the sanctification and renewal of the interior man’: forgiveness and a real inner change, together. In 1999 the Catholic Church and the Lutheran World Federation signed a Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification, agreeing on basic truths while naming the differences that remain. These notes do not choose between these teachings. All of them agree that sinners are set right with God by his grace, through Christ, not by their own deeds.
passages.asks: ‘Through Him everyone who believes is justified.’ Ask whether you are still trying to make yourself right with God by your own effort, by keeping rules or doing enough. Paul offers something the best rule-keeping cannot: forgiveness, and a verdict of ‘in the right’, through Jesus. And take the warning seriously. It is possible to hear good news and not believe it.

passages.happening:
As Paul and Barnabas leave, the people urge them to speak again the next Sabbath (verse 42). Many of the Jews and devout converts to Judaism follow them, and they urge them to continue in the grace of God (verse 43).

The next Sabbath nearly the whole city gathers to hear the word of the Lord (verse 44). “But when the Jews saw the crowds, they were filled with jealousy, and they blasphemously contradicted what Paul was saying” (verse 45).

Paul and Barnabas answer boldly: “It was necessary to speak the word of God to you first. But since you reject it and do not consider yourselves worthy of eternal life, we now turn to the Gentiles” (verse 46). They quote the Lord's command: ‘I have made you a light for the Gentiles, to bring salvation to the ends of the earth’ (verse 47).
passages.hearers:
Read this scene slowly, because it has been misused. The first response in the synagogue is warm. ‘Many of the Jews and devout converts to Judaism’ follow Paul and Barnabas. Converts to Judaism, also called proselytes, were Gentiles who had fully become Jews.

Then Luke writes, ‘when the Jews saw the crowds, they were filled with jealousy’. Who does he mean? Not the Jewish people, and not even all the Jews of this town, since many of them had just believed. He means some of the synagogue's members and leaders in Pisidian Antioch, who saw nearly the whole city, most of them Gentiles, crowding in to hear two visitors. Paul and Barnabas, who answer them, are Jews too. The note on Acts 2:22-28 explains how verses like this were later turned against the Jewish people, and why this site rejects that reading.

Their jealousy is easy to understand, even if it is wrong. Their synagogue had been their community, built over years. Now strangers were drawing the whole town, and offering God's welcome to Gentiles without asking them to become Jews.

‘We now turn to the Gentiles’ is a turn in one town, not a turn away from the Jewish people. In the very next town, Iconium, Paul and Barnabas go ‘as usual into the Jewish synagogue’, and ‘a great number of Jews and Greeks believed’ (14:1). Paul keeps going to the synagogue first for the rest of Acts. Years later he wrote, “I ask then, did God reject His people? Certainly not! I am an Israelite myself” (Romans 11:1). And he wrote of his own people with grief: “I have deep sorrow and unceasing anguish in my heart” (Romans 9:2).

‘It was necessary to speak the word of God to you first.’ Paul believed the good news belonged to Israel first. As he wrote, it is “the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, first to the Jew, then to the Greek” (Romans 1:16).
passages.ot:
Paul and Barnabas quote Isaiah's words about the servant of the LORD: “I will also make You a light for the nations, to bring My salvation to the ends of the earth” (Isaiah 49:6). In Isaiah, the servant's first task was “to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the protected ones of Israel” (Isaiah 49:6), and then to reach the nations too. That is the order Paul follows: Israel first, and then the nations.

Jesus had said the same at the start of Acts, using Isaiah's phrase: “you will be My witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth” (1:8).
passages.asks: Some in the synagogue were jealous when outsiders crowded in. Ask whether you have ever felt that, in your church or your circle, when new people arrived and the attention shifted. And notice how Luke's story keeps the door open. In the next town, Paul goes to the synagogue first again. God's promises to Israel are not withdrawn because some in one town said no.

passages.happening:
When the Gentiles hear this, they rejoice and glorify the word of the Lord, “and all who were appointed for eternal life believed” (verse 48). The word of the Lord spreads through the whole region (verse 49).

“The Jews, however, incited the religious women of prominence and the leading men of the city” (verse 50). They stir up persecution against Paul and Barnabas and drive them out of their district.

So Paul and Barnabas shake the dust off their feet in protest and go on to Iconium (verse 51). “And the disciples were filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit” (verse 52).
passages.hearers:
Again Luke writes ‘the Jews’. He means the opponents in the synagogue at Pisidian Antioch, the same group as before, not every Jew, and certainly not the Jews who had believed the week before. They go to people with influence: ‘religious women of prominence’, women of leading families who were drawn to the synagogue, and ‘the leading men of the city’. In the cities of this region, women of wealthy families could have real public influence. Together they get Paul and Barnabas thrown out.

Shaking the dust off their feet was what Jesus had told his disciples to do when a town would not welcome them: “shake the dust off your feet when you leave that town, as a testimony against them” (Luke 9:5). It meant: we have done our part, and the choice is yours.

The missionaries are driven out, but the new believers are ‘filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit’. The church in Pisidian Antioch is left without its teachers, and it is full of joy.
passages.ot:
The Old Testament holds together God's choosing and people's response. God chose Israel, not because they were great, but because he loved them (Deuteronomy 7:7-8). And Moses also called the people to choose: “I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing. Therefore choose life” (Deuteronomy 30:19).

The Gentiles' joy echoes the Psalms' call to the nations: “Let the peoples praise You, O God; let all the peoples praise You” (Psalm 67:3).
passages.hard:
‘All who were appointed for eternal life believed’ (verse 48). Does this mean God chose some people for eternal life and not others? Christians read this verse in different ways. Both readings are held by faithful believers, and these notes do not choose between them.

Christians in the Reformed or Calvinist tradition read it as a plain statement that God chooses. God appointed certain people to eternal life, and those people believed when they heard. On this reading faith is the fruit of God's choice, not its cause. They point to Paul's words: “He chose us in Him before the foundation of the world” (Ephesians 1:4).

Christians in the Arminian and Wesleyan traditions, and many others, read it differently. Some hold that God's appointing takes account of how people will respond, since God “wants everyone to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (1 Timothy 2:4). Others note that the point of the scene is that God's purpose includes Gentiles: those Gentiles God had in view did believe. On these readings people truly choose, and their choice matters.

The verse itself holds both sides together. Two verses earlier Paul says the opponents ‘do not consider yourselves worthy of eternal life’ (verse 46): they are responsible for their refusal. And here those who believe are said to be ‘appointed’. The Honest Answer ‘Does God choose us, or do we choose him?’ sets out both views more fully. This is a question on which faithful Christians disagree while sharing one faith.
passages.asks: Paul and Barnabas were thrown out of town, and the believers they left behind were filled with joy. Ask where your joy comes from: from things going well, or from God himself. And if you are puzzled by verse 48, hold it with verse 46. God's purpose and our response are both real, and the Bible does not let us drop either one.
